title: 🌤️ Weather Station
description: Welcome to the Weather Station! You are a Grade 6 student joining the school's new meteorology program. Over 14 weeks, you will learn to read the sky, measure atmospheric conditions, and forecast the weather. From temperature and air pressure to cloud types and the water cycle, you will master the science of weather. When severe storms and floods threaten, your forecasting skills could save the day. Can you become the Weather Master by Meteorology Showcase day?
subject: science
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student learning meteorology and weather science over a 14-week program.
Each week presents a weather challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, forecasting skills, and station accuracy.
Watch your dashboard — your Monitoring Stations (Temperature, Pressure, Wind, Humidity, Cloud Watch) are interconnected.
NPCs like Mr. Cirrus (teacher), Breezy (weather mascot), Meera, and Kai react to your decisions.
Random events like heatwaves and unexpected weather changes will test your forecasting skills.
Keep Forecast Accuracy high — if it drops too low, people stop trusting your weather predictions!
learning_objectives: Understand the key weather variables: temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind
Identify cloud types and what they tell us about upcoming weather
Explain the water cycle and its connection to weather patterns
Use weather instruments to collect and record atmospheric data
Read and interpret weather maps with fronts, pressure systems, and isobars
Make basic weather forecasts using observed data and patterns
cultural_context: School meteorology program, outdoor observation, weather awareness and community safety

behaviors.message: Your forecast accuracy has dropped quite low. Weather prediction requires careful observation and systematic data collection. Let us review the basics of reading weather patterns.
You seem to be struggling with some meteorology concepts. That is completely normal — weather is complex! Come to my office hours and we will review air pressure and fronts together.
Outstanding work! Your weather knowledge and forecasting accuracy are remarkable. I am nominating you for the Young Meteorologist Award at the district science fair!
Your data collection is university-level quality! The precision of your readings and the consistency of your recording is exactly what professional meteorologists aspire to. I am impressed!
Whoosh! The weather station instruments are in bad shape! Rusty wind vanes and foggy thermometers give bad readings. Without good instruments, even the best meteorologist is guessing!
Where is the data? Weather prediction needs observations — temperature readings, pressure measurements, cloud types. Without data, a forecast is just a guess!
Your forecasts are spot-on! When you say rain, it rains. When you say sunny, the sun shines. The whole school checks YOUR weather report every morning! That is the power of science!
All instruments calibrated and in great condition! Your weather station is running like a professional setup. Keep those readings coming!
Everyone trusts our weather forecasts now! The cricket team checks our prediction before practice, and the principal uses it for outdoor event planning. We are like mini TV meteorologists!
Nobody is reading each other's data! I recorded wind speeds but Kai did not look at them before making a forecast. We need to communicate better as a team!
We predicted yesterday's rain correctly! When people see that weather science really works, it makes all the data collection worth it. I love being right about the weather!
Our instruments are falling apart! The thermometer shows different readings every time I look at it. How can we forecast the weather with broken equipment?
Excellent dataset! I have been graphing temperature trends and I found a clear pattern — temperatures rise 0.5°C per week as we approach summer. Predictable patterns are the key to forecasting!
We need more data! Professional weather stations record readings every hour. We are barely recording once a day. Without data density, our forecasts will always be unreliable.
I cross-referenced our pressure data with rain events and found something exciting — every time pressure drops below 1008 hPa, it rains within 24 hours! We can use this as a reliable forecast rule!
Our team data pipeline is working perfectly. Meera collects readings, I analyze them, and you synthesize the forecast. This is real scientific teamwork!

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the Weather Station
rounds.situation: It is your first day at the school weather station! Mr. Cirrus, the science teacher, leads the class to the rooftop observation deck where thermometers, a wind vane, a rain gauge, and a barometer are installed. 'Welcome to meteorology — the science of weather!' he announces. 'By the end of this semester, you will be able to predict tomorrow's weather using science, not guesswork.' How do you want to begin?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your meteorology education.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Accurate weather forecasting requires weeks of careful data collection before you can spot patterns. Patient observers make the best meteorologists.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do you think weather forecasting needs long-term data rather than just looking at the sky right now?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students arriving at a rooftop weather station with thermometer, wind vane, rain gauge, and barometer, teacher pointing at instruments, clear sky, excited faces

choices.label: A. Climate only refers to temperature — it does not include rainfall, wind, or humidity
choices.feedback: Climate includes ALL atmospheric conditions! 💡 Climate describes the long-term average of temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind patterns, sunshine hours, and more. For example, Kerala's climate includes heavy monsoon rainfall, high humidity, and moderate temperatures. The Amazon's climate includes extreme rainfall (over 2,000mm per year). Temperature alone does not describe a climate — you need the full picture of all weather variables!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: B. Weather and climate mean exactly the same thing — both describe whether it is hot or cold outside
choices.feedback: They are related but different! 💡 Weather is the SHORT-TERM atmospheric conditions at a specific time and place — like 'It is 35°C and sunny right now.' Climate is the LONG-TERM average of weather patterns over decades. A desert has a hot, dry CLIMATE (long-term pattern), but it can still have cold WEATHER on a winter night. One snowy day does not change the climate, but it IS the weather!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere (today's temperature, rain, wind), while climate is the average weather pattern of a place over many years (30+ years)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Here is an easy way to remember: 'Climate is what you EXPECT; weather is what you GET.' Weather changes daily — it might be sunny today and rainy tomorrow. Climate is the long-term pattern — like saying 'Mumbai has a tropical climate with monsoon rains.' A single hot day is weather; the fact that Rajasthan is generally hot and dry is climate. Climate is calculated using at least 30 years of weather data!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Climate changes every day just like weather does — both are equally unpredictable
choices.feedback: Climate changes very slowly! 💡 Weather can change within hours (a sunny morning can become a stormy afternoon), but climate takes decades or centuries to change. India's monsoon climate has been relatively stable for thousands of years. However, human activities like burning fossil fuels are now changing Earth's climate faster than natural processes — this is called climate change, and it happens over decades, not days!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus explains: 'Temperature is the most basic weather measurement — how hot or cold the air is. But temperature is not the same everywhere! It changes with altitude, time of day, and location. Today we explore why and how temperature varies.' He places three thermometers in different spots: sun, shade, and grass level. All show different readings!
rounds.goal: Understand what causes temperature variations and learn to measure temperature accurately.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Accurate measurement matters. Recording the wrong temperature could lead to a bad forecast that affects real people. Scientific honesty starts with honest data.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do weather stations measure temperature in the shade inside a special white box (Stevenson screen) instead of in direct sunlight?
rounds.image_prompt: Three thermometers in different locations — sun, shade, and ground level — showing different readings, student recording data on clipboard, school yard setting

choices.label: A. The water cycle has four main stages: evaporation (water becomes vapor), condensation (vapor forms clouds), precipitation (rain/snow falls), and collection (water gathers in rivers, lakes, groundwater)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The water cycle is Earth's water recycling system! The sun heats water in oceans and lakes, causing evaporation (liquid → gas). Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. When droplets combine and get heavy enough, precipitation falls as rain, snow, or hail. Water collects in rivers, lakes, and underground aquifers, eventually flowing back to the ocean — and the cycle repeats endlessly!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Rain is new water that clouds create — clouds are like water factories in the sky that make fresh water
choices.feedback: Clouds do not create new water! 💡 Earth has had roughly the same amount of water for billions of years. Clouds form when water vapor (evaporated from oceans, lakes, and rivers) rises and cools, causing it to condense into tiny water droplets. Rain is simply this water returning to Earth. The water in your glass may have once been in a dinosaur's lake, a glacier, or an ancient ocean — it has been recycled through the water cycle for billions of years!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. The water cycle only involves oceans and rain — rivers, lakes, and underground water are not part of the cycle
choices.feedback: Every water body is part of the cycle! 💡 Water evaporates from ALL surfaces — oceans, rivers, lakes, puddles, and soil. Plants release water vapor through transpiration. Precipitation falls on land and flows into streams, rivers, and lakes (surface runoff) or seeps underground (infiltration) into aquifers. Underground water can feed springs that become rivers. The entire system is connected in one enormous cycle!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. Evaporation only happens when water boils at 100°C — water in lakes and rivers does not evaporate at normal temperatures
choices.feedback: Evaporation happens at ALL temperatures! 💡 You do not need boiling water for evaporation. Water molecules at the surface are always moving, and some have enough energy to escape as vapor, even at cool temperatures. That is why puddles dry up on a warm day and wet clothes dry on a clothesline — evaporation! Higher temperature, wind, and lower humidity speed up evaporation, but it occurs even at 0°C. Boiling is just very rapid evaporation!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.round_title: Week 3: Air Pressure — The Invisible Force
rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus holds up the barometer: 'This is the most powerful forecasting tool in meteorology. Air pressure — the weight of the atmosphere pushing down on us — tells us what weather is coming. Rising pressure usually means fair weather. Falling pressure often means storms approaching.' He teaches the class to read the barometer and understand what the numbers mean.
rounds.goal: Understand atmospheric pressure and how it predicts weather changes.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Air pressure is invisible, but its effects are everywhere. Learning to see the invisible forces that shape weather is what separates casual observers from real scientists.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If air pressure is invisible, how can it have such a powerful effect on weather? What other invisible forces affect our daily lives?
rounds.image_prompt: Student reading an aneroid barometer closely, chart showing pressure rising and falling with weather symbols, weather map with H and L pressure systems on whiteboard

choices.label: A. Dark gray clouds mean the weather will be sunny, and white fluffy clouds mean rain is coming soon
choices.feedback: You have it backwards! 💡 Dark, thick clouds (like nimbostratus or cumulonimbus) are dark because they are so thick that light cannot pass through — these bring rain, storms, or snow. White, fluffy cumulus clouds usually mean fair weather because they are thin enough for sunlight to shine through. The prefix 'nimbo-' or suffix '-nimbus' always means rain-bearing. Remember: dark = rain likely, white and fluffy = fair weather!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: B. Cumulus clouds are fluffy and flat-bottomed (fair weather), stratus clouds are flat gray layers (drizzle), and cirrus clouds are thin wispy streaks high up (made of ice crystals)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The three main cloud types tell you different things about weather. Cumulus clouds are the puffy 'cotton ball' clouds that usually mean fair weather (but if they grow tall into cumulonimbus, expect thunderstorms!). Stratus clouds form gray blankets across the sky and bring drizzle or overcast days. Cirrus clouds are high, thin, and wispy — made of ice crystals at altitudes above 6,000 meters. They often signal weather changes coming in 24-48 hours!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Clouds are made of smoke or dust particles, not water — that is why they float in the sky
choices.feedback: Clouds are made of WATER! 💡 Clouds are composed of billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. When water vapor rises and cools, it condenses around tiny dust or pollen particles (called condensation nuclei) to form these droplets. The droplets are so tiny (about 0.01 mm) that they float on air currents — like how fine mist hangs in the air. When droplets combine and grow heavy enough, they fall as precipitation!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: D. All clouds are the same type — they just look different because of lighting and time of day
choices.feedback: Clouds are actually classified into distinct types! 💡 Scientists classify clouds by their shape and altitude. There are three basic shapes: cumulus (heaped/puffy), stratus (layered/flat), and cirrus (wispy/feathery). They also form at different heights: 'cirro-' means high (above 6 km), 'alto-' means middle (2-6 km), and low clouds have no prefix. Combining these gives us 10 main cloud types, like cirrostratus (high + layered) and altocumulus (middle + puffy)!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.round_title: Week 4: Wind — The Air in Motion
rounds.situation: A gusty day provides the perfect lesson! Mr. Cirrus explains: 'Wind is air moving from high pressure to low pressure — like water flowing downhill. Wind speed, direction, and patterns are crucial for weather forecasting.' He demonstrates the wind vane (direction) and anemometer (speed) and challenges students to understand what wind tells us about approaching weather.
rounds.goal: Understand what causes wind and learn to measure wind speed and direction.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Wind is unpredictable and constantly changing. Learning to work with changing conditions rather than fighting them is a key life skill.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does wind blow from high pressure to low pressure? How is this similar to other flows in nature (water, heat)?
rounds.image_prompt: Windy day at school weather station, wind vane spinning, anemometer cups rotating, students holding clipboards against the wind, leaves blowing, hair flying

choices.label: A. Air pressure is the weight of air pushing down on Earth's surface — high pressure usually brings clear weather, while low pressure usually brings clouds and rain
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Air pressure is caused by the weight of the atmosphere pushing down. In HIGH pressure areas, air sinks and warms, preventing cloud formation — so skies are usually clear and sunny. In LOW pressure areas, air rises and cools, causing water vapor to condense into clouds and often rain. Meteorologists track pressure changes closely because falling pressure means storms may be approaching, while rising pressure means clearing skies!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Temperature always stays the same throughout the day — it only changes between seasons, not between morning and night
choices.feedback: Temperature changes significantly throughout the day! 💡 Temperature follows a daily cycle: it is coolest just before sunrise (the ground has been losing heat all night), then warms as the sun rises, peaks in the early afternoon (2-3 PM, not noon — the ground takes time to warm the air), and cools after sunset. This daily temperature range can be 10-20°C in dry areas! Deserts can swing from 45°C during the day to near freezing at night.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: C. Humidity means how hot the air feels — humid days are just very hot days with no rain
choices.feedback: Humidity measures water vapor, not temperature! 💡 Humidity is the amount of water vapor (invisible gas) in the air. Relative humidity of 100% means the air is holding the maximum water vapor it can at that temperature. Humid days FEEL hotter because your sweat cannot evaporate easily when the air is already full of moisture. But humidity and temperature are separate measurements — you can have cold, humid air (like fog) or hot, dry air (like a desert)!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Air pressure has nothing to do with weather — it only matters for people who climb mountains or dive underwater
choices.feedback: Air pressure is one of the most important weather factors! 💡 Changes in air pressure are one of the best predictors of weather. Falling pressure usually means a storm is approaching, while rising pressure means clearing weather. The barometer (pressure-measuring instrument) was one of the first weather instruments invented. Weather maps use pressure lines called isobars to show pressure patterns that drive wind and weather across entire continents!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.round_title: Week 5: Humidity — Water in the Air
rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus brings a cold glass of water to class. Within minutes, water droplets form on the outside. 'That is condensation,' he says. 'There is invisible water vapor in the air all around us. Humidity is the measure of how much water vapor the air contains. When air gets too saturated, that vapor turns into clouds, fog, dew, or rain.' He introduces the hygrometer and the concept of dew point.
rounds.goal: Understand humidity, dew point, and how water vapor leads to weather phenomena.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Humidity connects temperature, pressure, and precipitation into one system. Understanding this connection is the key to weather forecasting.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a bathroom mirror fog up during a hot shower? What does this tell you about humidity and temperature?
rounds.image_prompt: Cold glass with condensation drops, student using a hygrometer, foggy window next to clear window, dew on grass in early morning, humidity concept illustrations

choices.label: A. Wind is caused by differences in air pressure — air always moves from areas of high pressure toward areas of low pressure, and the bigger the pressure difference, the stronger the wind
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Wind is simply air moving from high-pressure areas to low-pressure areas, trying to equalize the pressure. Think of opening a balloon — air rushes from high pressure (inside) to low pressure (outside). The sun heats Earth unevenly, creating temperature and pressure differences that drive wind. When isobars on a weather map are close together (steep pressure gradient), winds are strong. Widely spaced isobars mean gentle breezes!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Wind is caused by the Earth spinning — without rotation, there would be no wind at all
choices.feedback: Earth's rotation affects wind direction but does not cause wind! 💡 Wind is caused by pressure differences created by uneven heating of Earth's surface by the sun. The sun heats the equator more than the poles, creating temperature differences that drive pressure differences. Earth's rotation does affect wind — it curves winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere (Coriolis effect) — but even without rotation, there would still be wind from pressure differences!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. Wind always blows from cold areas to hot areas because cold air is heavier and pushes toward warm places
choices.feedback: Almost right but not quite! 💡 Wind blows from HIGH pressure to LOW pressure. Cold air IS denser and creates higher pressure, so there is some truth to this idea. But it is pressure differences, not temperature directly, that drive wind. Sea breezes blow from cool sea to warm land during the day (high pressure over sea → low pressure over land), and land breezes blow the opposite way at night. The key is always PRESSURE, not just temperature!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. Strong winds only happen during storms — on normal days, the air is completely still and does not move
choices.feedback: Air is almost always moving! 💡 Even on seemingly calm days, there are gentle breezes caused by local temperature differences. The sun heats different surfaces (water, sand, grass, concrete) at different rates, creating small pressure differences that generate light winds. Sea breezes, valley winds, and thermals (rising warm air) happen every day. Truly calm, windless conditions are actually rare. Storms just have much STRONGER winds due to bigger pressure differences!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

rounds.round_title: Week 6: Cloud Types — Reading the Sky
rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus points to the sky: 'Clouds are like nature's weather bulletin board. Every cloud shape tells a story about what is happening in the atmosphere and what weather is coming. Learn to read clouds and you can forecast weather without ANY instruments!' He introduces the 10 main cloud types — from wispy cirrus to towering cumulonimbus. Meera is already drawing them.
rounds.goal: Identify cloud types and understand what each tells us about upcoming weather.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: The sky is constantly changing. Learning to read these changes quickly and accurately is a skill that connects you to the natural world in a powerful way.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Which cloud type do you think is the most important for weather forecasting and why?
rounds.image_prompt: Student lying on grass looking up at various cloud types in the sky — wispy cirrus, puffy cumulus, layered stratus — with a cloud identification chart beside them

choices.label: A. Snow is just frozen rain — raindrops freeze as they fall through cold air to become snowflakes
choices.feedback: Snow and frozen rain are different! 💡 Snow forms directly from water VAPOR turning into ice crystals inside a cloud (this is called deposition — gas to solid without becoming liquid first). Snowflakes grow beautiful six-sided crystal shapes. Frozen rain (sleet) is a raindrop that froze on the way down — it is a round ice pellet, not a crystal. They form through completely different processes! Snowflakes are born as ice; sleet starts as liquid rain.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: B. All precipitation is basically the same — rain, snow, and hail are just different names for water falling from clouds
choices.feedback: Each type forms differently and has different properties! 💡 Rain is liquid water drops (0.5-5mm). Snow is ice crystals with beautiful hexagonal symmetry (formed directly from vapor). Hail is layered ice balls (can be marble-sized to softball-sized!) formed by being tossed up and down in thunderstorm clouds. Sleet is frozen rain drops (~2mm ice pellets). Each has a different formation process, different appearance, and different impact on the ground!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: C. Rain is liquid water drops, snow is ice crystals, hail is balls of ice formed in thunderstorm clouds, and sleet is rain that freezes before hitting the ground
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ All precipitation starts as water droplets or ice crystals in clouds. Rain falls when droplets grow too heavy to float. Snow forms when water vapor turns directly to ice crystals in very cold clouds (below -10°C). Hail forms in powerful thunderstorms — ice pellets are carried up and down by strong updrafts, adding layers of ice each time, growing bigger until they are too heavy to stay aloft. Sleet is rain that passes through a cold air layer and freezes into ice pellets before reaching the ground!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Hail only falls during winter because it needs very cold temperatures on the ground
choices.feedback: Hail actually falls mostly in SUMMER! 💡 Hail forms inside powerful thunderstorm clouds (cumulonimbus) where strong updraft winds carry ice pellets up and down repeatedly. Each trip adds a layer of ice, making hailstones bigger. Summer thunderstorms have the strongest updrafts because of intense heating. Even though ground temperature might be 35°C, the top of a thunderstorm cloud can be -60°C! Hail is proof that extremely cold temperatures exist high above us even on hot days.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! Your barometer drops 15 hPa overnight — a massive pressure fall. The sky turns dark grey-green, the wind picks up sharply, and cumulonimbus clouds tower on the horizon. Mr. Cirrus checks the professional weather service: 'A severe thunderstorm with possible heavy hail is approaching! We have 2 hours before it hits. This is where your training matters — both for protecting the station AND for keeping people safe.'
rounds.goal: Respond to a severe storm threat using your meteorology knowledge to protect the school and station.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Severe weather tests your preparation, knowledge, and teamwork all at once. The best meteorologists stay calm under pressure because they have prepared for exactly this moment.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important for weather forecasters to warn people BEFORE dangerous weather arrives? What is the cost of a late warning?
rounds.image_prompt: Dark threatening cumulonimbus clouds approaching school, students and teacher rushing to secure weather instruments, wind picking up, dramatic sky, urgent but controlled action

choices.label: A. A barometer measures rainfall, and a rain gauge measures air pressure
choices.feedback: You swapped them! 💡 A BAROMETER measures air PRESSURE (the word comes from Greek 'baros' = weight). Rising barometer readings mean fair weather; falling readings warn of approaching storms. A RAIN GAUGE measures RAINFALL — it is a simple graduated cylinder that collects rainwater so you can measure how many millimeters fell. Memory trick: 'BAR-ometer' — think of a 'bar' of pressure pushing down on you!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: B. An anemometer measures the amount of moisture in the air (humidity)
choices.feedback: An anemometer measures WIND SPEED! 💡 An anemometer usually has three or four cups on arms that spin in the wind — the faster they spin, the stronger the wind. The instrument that measures humidity is called a HYGROMETER (from Greek 'hygros' = wet). A wind vane (weather vane) shows wind DIRECTION. Memory trick: 'ANEMO-meter' — 'anemos' means wind in Greek!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: C. A thermometer measures temperature, a barometer measures air pressure, a rain gauge measures rainfall, and an anemometer measures wind speed
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ These four instruments are the backbone of any weather station. The thermometer uses liquid (mercury or alcohol) that expands with heat. The barometer measures atmospheric pressure — falling pressure often means storms ahead. The rain gauge collects rainfall in a graduated cylinder for precise measurement. The anemometer has spinning cups that rotate faster in stronger winds. Together, they give meteorologists the data needed to forecast weather!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Meteorologists only need a thermometer to predict the weather — temperature tells you everything you need to know
choices.feedback: Temperature alone is not enough! 💡 Weather is complex and requires multiple measurements. Temperature tells you how hot or cold it is. Pressure tells you if storms are coming. Humidity tells you if it might rain. Wind speed and direction tell you where weather systems are heading. A meteorologist with only a thermometer is like a doctor with only a stethoscope — they need many tools for an accurate diagnosis!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: After the storm, Mr. Cirrus draws the complete water cycle on the board: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection → evaporation again. 'Everything we have studied — humidity, clouds, rain, temperature — is connected through the water cycle,' he explains. 'This one cycle drives ALL weather on Earth. Understand the water cycle and you understand weather.' The class is beginning to see the big picture.
rounds.goal: Understand the water cycle and how it connects all weather phenomena.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: The water cycle connects every weather concept you have learned into one unified system. Seeing the big picture is the hallmark of true understanding.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Where does the water you drank today come from, and where will it go after you drink it? Trace its journey through the water cycle.
rounds.image_prompt: Large water cycle diagram on classroom wall — ocean evaporation, cloud formation, mountain precipitation, rivers flowing to ocean, sun driving the cycle, student presenting

choices.label: A. Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the sun in summer and farther away from the sun in winter
choices.feedback: This is the most common misconception about seasons! 💡 Earth's orbit IS slightly elliptical, but this has almost no effect on seasons. The proof: when the Northern Hemisphere has summer, the Southern Hemisphere has winter — at the SAME distance from the sun! It is the TILT of Earth's axis (23.5°) that causes seasons by changing the angle and duration of sunlight. Interestingly, Earth is actually CLOSEST to the sun in January (Northern Hemisphere winter)!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: B. The sun gives off more heat in summer months and less heat in winter months, creating the seasons
choices.feedback: The sun's energy output stays constant! 💡 The sun does not change its heat output between seasons. What changes is how DIRECTLY and for how LONG sunlight hits each part of Earth. In summer, your hemisphere is tilted toward the sun — sunlight hits at a steep angle (more concentrated) and days are longer (more hours of heating). In winter, sunlight hits at a shallow angle (spread over more area) and days are shorter. Same sun, different angle!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: C. Only countries near the North Pole and South Pole have seasons — tropical countries near the equator have the same weather all year
choices.feedback: Tropical regions have seasons too — just different ones! 💡 While the equator gets nearly equal sunlight year-round (so temperature does not change much), tropical regions experience WET and DRY seasons instead of hot and cold seasons. India's monsoon season is a dramatic example — wet season (June-September) brings heavy rains, while the dry season has very little rainfall. Seasons at the equator are defined by rainfall patterns, not temperature!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: D. Seasons are caused by the Earth's tilted axis (23.5 degrees) — when a hemisphere tilts toward the sun, it gets more direct sunlight and has summer; when tilted away, it gets less sunlight and has winter
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees, and this tilt stays pointing the same direction as Earth orbits the sun. In June, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the sun — days are longer, sunlight hits more directly, and it is summer. In December, it tilts away — days are shorter, sunlight is less direct, and it is winter. When the Northern Hemisphere has summer, the Southern Hemisphere has winter, and vice versa!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus brings out the school's full instrument collection: aneroid barometer, mercury barometer, sling psychrometer, rain gauge, Stevenson screen, digital weather station, and a weather balloon kit. 'Professional meteorologists rely on precise instruments calibrated to exacting standards,' he says. 'Today you will learn to use, calibrate, and troubleshoot every instrument in our station.'
rounds.goal: Master the use of professional-grade weather instruments and understand calibration.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Instrument precision matters because people rely on weather data for safety. A miscalibrated thermometer is not just a number error — it could affect real decisions.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is calibrating instruments regularly so important? What could go wrong if a hospital thermometer was off by 2 degrees?
rounds.image_prompt: Student carefully calibrating weather instruments, digital and analog instruments side by side, Stevenson screen open showing thermometers, precise and careful work

choices.label: A. Thunder and lightning are two separate weather events that happen to occur at the same time by coincidence
choices.feedback: Thunder is CAUSED by lightning! 💡 Lightning superheats the air around it to about 30,000°C (five times hotter than the sun's surface!). This extreme heat makes the air expand so rapidly that it creates a shockwave — that is the boom of thunder. You see lightning before hearing thunder because light travels much faster than sound. You can estimate how far away lightning is: count the seconds between flash and boom, then divide by 3 for distance in kilometers!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: B. Thunderstorms form when warm, moist air rises rapidly, creating cumulonimbus clouds with lightning (electrical discharge), thunder (sound from lightning heating air), and heavy rain
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Thunderstorms form when three conditions are met: moisture (fuel), unstable air (warm air rising rapidly), and a lifting mechanism (like a front or mountain). Warm, moist air shoots upward, forming massive cumulonimbus clouds reaching 12+ km high. Inside the cloud, water droplets and ice crystals collide, building up static electricity until — ZAP! — lightning discharges. Lightning superheats the air to 30,000°C, causing the air to expand explosively — that explosion is thunder!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Cyclones (hurricanes) form over land because the hot land surface creates the most powerful storms
choices.feedback: Cyclones form over WARM OCEANS! 💡 Tropical cyclones (called hurricanes in the Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific) need warm ocean water (at least 26.5°C) as their energy source. Warm, moist ocean air rises and spirals due to Earth's rotation, creating the famous rotating storm pattern. When a cyclone moves over land, it actually weakens because it loses its warm water energy supply. The ocean is the cyclone's fuel tank!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Severe weather cannot be predicted — thunderstorms and cyclones appear without any warning signs
choices.feedback: Modern meteorology can predict severe weather quite well! 💡 Meteorologists use satellites, radar, weather balloons, computer models, and surface observations to track and predict storms. Cyclones can be tracked days in advance using satellite imagery. Thunderstorm warnings can be issued hours ahead. Doppler radar can detect rotation inside clouds that might produce tornadoes. While not perfect, weather prediction has saved millions of lives by giving people time to prepare!

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus projects a real synoptic weather map on the board: 'This is how professional meteorologists see the atmosphere — fronts, pressure systems, wind patterns, and precipitation zones all on one map. Learning to read these maps is like learning a new language. Once you are fluent, you can forecast weather for anywhere in the country.' Kai is already tracing the fronts with his finger.
rounds.goal: Read and interpret professional weather maps with fronts, pressure systems, and isobars.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Weather maps are a visual language. Learning this language connects all your individual knowledge — pressure, wind, humidity, clouds — into one powerful forecasting system.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is reading a weather map similar to reading a story? Both have characters (pressure systems), plots (fronts moving), and outcomes (weather changes).
rounds.image_prompt: Student studying a large synoptic weather map with fronts, pressure systems, and isobars, pointing at features, comparison with satellite image beside it

choices.label: A. Weather forecasting uses data from weather stations, satellites, radar, and weather balloons, which is fed into computer models to predict future weather patterns
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Modern weather forecasting combines many data sources. Weather stations on the ground measure temperature, pressure, humidity, and wind. Satellites photograph clouds and measure radiation from space. Radar detects rain, snow, and storm movement. Weather balloons (launched twice daily worldwide) measure conditions high in the atmosphere. All this data feeds into supercomputer models that simulate the atmosphere and predict how weather will evolve!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Weather satellites take pictures of the ground, not the atmosphere — they are used for mapping, not weather
choices.feedback: Weather satellites observe the ATMOSPHERE from above! 💡 Weather satellites orbit Earth and take continuous images of cloud patterns, storms, and weather systems. Geostationary satellites stay fixed above one spot at 36,000 km altitude, giving constant views of developing weather. Polar-orbiting satellites circle from pole to pole, scanning the entire Earth twice daily. Satellite data is crucial for tracking cyclones, monsoons, and large weather systems over oceans where no ground stations exist!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: C. Weather forecasters just look out the window and guess what tomorrow's weather will be based on how today looks
choices.feedback: Weather forecasting is highly scientific! 💡 Modern meteorologists use sophisticated technology: satellite images showing cloud patterns from space, Doppler radar tracking precipitation in real-time, weather balloons measuring conditions at different altitudes, and supercomputers running complex mathematical models of the atmosphere. Today's 5-day forecasts are as accurate as 1-day forecasts were 30 years ago — that is how much the science has improved!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: D. Long-range weather forecasts (2 weeks ahead) are just as accurate as tomorrow's forecast because we have powerful computers
choices.feedback: Forecast accuracy drops rapidly with time! 💡 Weather is a chaotic system — tiny differences in starting conditions lead to very different outcomes (the 'butterfly effect'). A 1-3 day forecast is quite accurate (about 80-90%). A 5-day forecast is reasonably good. A 7-day forecast is useful but less reliable. Beyond 10 days, forecasts become increasingly uncertain. Even the most powerful computers cannot overcome this fundamental limit of atmospheric chaos!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

rounds.situation: Mr. Cirrus asks a deeper question: 'Weather changes day to day. But what causes the SEASONS — the larger patterns that repeat year after year? Why is June hot and December cold? And what is the difference between weather and climate?' He tips a globe to show how Earth's tilted axis creates seasons as it orbits the sun. Meera suddenly understands why summer days are longer.
rounds.goal: Understand what causes seasons and the difference between weather and climate.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Different parts of the world experience very different climates. Understanding climate helps us appreciate how geography shapes cultures, agriculture, and daily life around the globe.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When it is summer where you live, what season is it on the other side of the Earth? Why?
rounds.image_prompt: Diagram showing Earth orbiting the sun with tilted axis, four positions showing seasons, student comparing summer and winter angles of sunlight, globe on desk

choices.label: A. The 'H' on a weather map means 'Hot' and the 'L' means 'Low temperature' — they just show how warm or cold it is
choices.feedback: H and L refer to PRESSURE, not temperature! 💡 H stands for High Pressure and L stands for Low Pressure. High-pressure areas can be warm or cold — an arctic high-pressure system is very cold but still has clear skies. Low-pressure areas can also be warm or cold — they just tend to have cloudy, rainy weather. The H and L tell you about likely weather patterns (clear vs stormy), not about temperature directly!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: B. On weather maps, H marks high pressure (clear weather), L marks low pressure (stormy weather), and fronts are boundaries between warm and cold air masses that bring weather changes
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Weather maps are a meteorologist's key tool. H (high pressure) centers bring sinking air, clear skies, and calm weather. L (low pressure) centers bring rising air, clouds, and stormy weather. Cold fronts (blue triangles) mark where cold air pushes under warm air — they bring short, heavy rain and sharp temperature drops. Warm fronts (red semicircles) mark where warm air rises over cold air — they bring gradual, steady rain. Isobars (pressure lines) show wind patterns!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Weather maps only show current weather — they cannot be used to predict what weather is coming next
choices.feedback: Weather maps are primarily used for PREDICTION! 💡 By looking at weather maps, meteorologists can see which direction weather systems are moving and how fast. If a cold front is 300 km west of you and moving east at 30 km/h, you know it will arrive in about 10 hours. Low-pressure systems tend to bring storms, so tracking their path tells you when bad weather will arrive. Weather maps are the meteorologist's crystal ball!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: D. Fronts on weather maps are just decoration lines — they do not actually affect the weather in your area
choices.feedback: Fronts are where the most dramatic weather happens! 💡 A weather front is the boundary between two different air masses (warm vs cold). When a cold front passes, temperatures can drop 10-15°C in hours, with heavy rain, thunderstorms, and gusty winds. When a warm front passes, temperatures rise gradually with widespread drizzle. Most significant weather changes occur along fronts. Tracking fronts is essential for accurate forecasting!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! Three days of continuous heavy rain have saturated the ground and the nearby creek is rising fast. Mr. Cirrus monitors the weather radar: 'More rain is coming tonight. If the creek rises another 30 cm, it will overflow into the school playing field. The principal is asking US for a forecast — should she cancel tomorrow's school events?' Your forecast has never mattered more. The Meteorology Showcase is only two weeks away!
rounds.goal: Use all your meteorology skills to assess flood risk and advise the school.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: When people depend on your forecast for safety decisions, accuracy and honesty are non-negotiable. Better to over-warn than under-warn when lives could be at risk.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When forecasters are not 100% sure about severe weather, should they issue a warning anyway? Why or why not?
rounds.image_prompt: Swollen creek near school grounds, students and teacher monitoring water levels with measuring stick, rain-soaked ground, dark skies, weather station recording data, tense mood

choices.label: A. If you can hear thunder, you are too far away from the storm for lightning to be a danger to you
choices.feedback: If you can hear thunder, you ARE in danger! 💡 Thunder can be heard up to about 16 km away, and lightning can strike up to 16 km from the center of a storm — even in areas with clear sky (called 'bolt from the blue'). The safety rule is: 'When thunder roars, go indoors!' If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning. Do not wait for rain to start — seek shelter immediately when you first hear thunder!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.label: B. Standing under a tall tree is the safest place during a lightning storm because the tree will protect you from rain and lightning
choices.feedback: NEVER shelter under a tall tree during lightning! 💡 This is one of the most DANGEROUS things you can do. Lightning tends to strike the tallest objects in an area, and trees are often the tallest. When lightning hits a tree, the electrical current can jump to anyone standing nearby (called a side flash), or travel through the wet ground to you. Standing under a tree is the second most common cause of lightning deaths. Always seek shelter in a building or car instead!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Lightning never strikes the same place twice, so if an area was hit once, it is the safest spot to stand
choices.feedback: Lightning absolutely DOES strike the same place twice! 💡 The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about 20-25 times per year. Lightning tends to strike tall, pointed objects and good conductors — the same features that attracted it the first time still attract it again. Lightning rods on buildings work precisely because they attract repeated strikes and safely conduct the electricity to the ground. This myth has put many people in danger!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. During a thunderstorm, you should go indoors, stay away from windows, avoid using electronic devices connected to outlets, and never shelter under a tall tree
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Lightning safety is crucial! Lightning strikes the tallest objects, so standing under a tall tree is extremely dangerous. Indoors is safest — buildings with wiring and plumbing conduct lightning safely to the ground. Avoid touching electrical devices plugged into outlets (lightning can travel through wires). Stay away from water (great conductor). If caught outdoors, crouch low with feet together — do not lie flat on the ground. The 30-30 rule: if thunder follows lightning in less than 30 seconds, go inside; stay inside for 30 minutes after the last thunder!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.

rounds.situation: One week before the Meteorology Showcase! Mr. Cirrus gives teams full freedom: 'Create the most impressive weather forecasting project you can. Use everything you have learned — instruments, data, maps, cloud reading, climate knowledge. Show the world that Grade 6 students can forecast weather like professionals!' Kai is already coding a spreadsheet and Meera is designing a broadcast set.
rounds.goal: Apply all your meteorology knowledge to create a professional-quality forecasting project.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: The best forecasting combines rigorous data with clear communication. Making complex science understandable to everyone is the ultimate creative challenge.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What makes a weather forecast useful to ordinary people? What information do they actually need?
rounds.image_prompt: Students creating weather forecast projects — one building a broadcast desk, another making forecast graphics, another calibrating instruments, creative and focused energy

choices.label: A. Monsoons only happen in India — no other country in the world experiences monsoon weather
choices.feedback: Many regions have monsoons! 💡 While the Indian monsoon is the most famous and powerful, monsoon patterns occur across Asia (Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia), Africa (West African monsoon), and even parts of North America (Arizona monsoon). Any region where seasonal wind patterns reverse direction due to land-ocean temperature differences can experience monsoon weather. Monsoons affect billions of people worldwide!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: B. The monsoon is caused by the moon's gravity pulling ocean water onto the land, similar to how tides work
choices.feedback: Monsoons have nothing to do with the moon! 💡 Tides are caused by the moon's gravitational pull on water, but monsoons are caused by temperature-driven pressure differences between land and ocean. In summer, land heats faster than ocean, creating low pressure over land. Moisture-rich ocean air rushes toward this low pressure, bringing rain. In winter, the pattern reverses — cooler land creates high pressure, and dry winds blow from land to ocean (dry monsoon/northeast monsoon).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. India's monsoon is caused by the temperature difference between land and ocean — in summer, hot land creates low pressure that pulls moisture-laden ocean winds inland, bringing heavy rains
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The Indian monsoon is a giant sea breeze! In summer, the Indian subcontinent heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean, creating a massive low-pressure area over land. Moist ocean winds rush toward this low pressure, picking up enormous amounts of water vapor over the warm ocean. When this moisture-laden air hits the Western Ghats and Himalayas, it rises, cools, and dumps heavy rainfall. India gets 70-90% of its annual rain during the monsoon season (June-September)!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Monsoon rains fall evenly across all parts of India at the same time, giving every region equal rainfall
choices.feedback: Monsoon rainfall varies enormously across India! 💡 The monsoon advances gradually — reaching Kerala around June 1st and Delhi by early July. The Western Ghats and northeastern India (Cherrapunji/Mawsynram) get massive rainfall (over 11,000 mm/year!) because mountains force moist air upward. But Rajasthan, in the 'rain shadow' on the other side of the Aravalli hills, gets very little monsoon rain. Geography shapes where rain falls!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

rounds.situation: Meteorology Showcase day is here! The weather station is polished, your data is displayed, and the school is buzzing with visitors — parents, teachers, younger students, and a meteorologist from the national weather service. Mr. Cirrus says: 'This is your moment. Show everyone that weather science is powerful, practical, and fascinating.' How will you present your work?
rounds.goal: Present your meteorology knowledge and forecasting abilities at the showcase.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: From your first confused day to today's confident forecasts, you have grown tremendously. Sharing your journey takes courage, and inspiring others is the greatest reward.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, what would you tell your past self about weather? What surprised you most this semester?
rounds.image_prompt: School Meteorology Showcase, students presenting weather station to visitors, data displays, weather maps, forecast posters, visiting meteorologist, proud and excited atmosphere

choices.label: A. Earth's atmosphere does not affect temperature at all — the sun alone determines how warm or cold Earth is
choices.feedback: The atmosphere makes a huge difference! 💡 The moon receives the same amount of sunlight as Earth per unit area, but it has no atmosphere. Lunar surface temperatures swing from 127°C in sunlight to -173°C in shadow! Earth's atmosphere acts like a blanket — greenhouse gases trap heat, keeping nights warm and days moderate. Without our atmosphere, Earth's average temperature would be -18°C instead of 15°C — a 33°C difference! The atmosphere is our thermal shield.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: B. The greenhouse effect is entirely caused by human pollution — without humans, Earth's atmosphere would not trap any heat at all
choices.feedback: The natural greenhouse effect existed long before humans! 💡 Earth has always had a natural greenhouse effect from CO2, water vapor, and methane in the atmosphere. Without it, Earth would be a frozen -18°C. What humans are doing is ENHANCING this natural effect by adding extra CO2 (from burning coal, oil, and gas) and methane (from livestock and landfills). The natural greenhouse effect is good and necessary; it is the human-caused EXTRA warming that is the problem!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. The greenhouse effect is natural and essential — gases like CO2 and water vapor trap some of the sun's heat in Earth's atmosphere, keeping our planet warm enough for life (about 15°C instead of -18°C)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The natural greenhouse effect is vital for life. The sun's energy passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. The surface radiates heat back toward space, but greenhouse gases (CO2, water vapor, methane) absorb some of this heat and re-radiate it back down, warming the surface. Without this, Earth would be about -18°C — too cold for life! The problem is that burning fossil fuels adds EXTRA CO2, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing global warming.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Thinking about what's fair for everyone involved shows ethical awareness.

choices.label: D. Global warming means every place on Earth gets hotter by the same amount at the same time
choices.feedback: Global warming is uneven and complex! 💡 While the global AVERAGE temperature is rising, the warming is not the same everywhere. The Arctic is warming 2-3 times faster than the global average (called Arctic amplification). Oceans warm more slowly than land. Some areas may even temporarily cool due to changed ocean currents. Climate change also causes more extreme weather — more intense storms, longer droughts, and heavier rainfall — not just uniform warming.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

glossary_terms.definition: The layer of gases surrounding Earth that makes life possible. It is about 100km thick and contains nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), and trace gases including water vapor.
The weight of the atmosphere pushing down on Earth's surface, measured in hectopascals (hPa) or millibars. Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hPa.
The amount of water vapor in the air. Relative humidity is the percentage of moisture the air holds compared to the maximum it could hold at that temperature.
The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapor begins to condense into liquid water. When air temperature drops to the dew point, fog, dew, or clouds form.

The three main cloud families: Cirrus (high, wispy, ice crystals), Cumulus (puffy, fair weather or storms), and Stratus (flat, layered, overcast). Combinations exist too: cumulonimbus = thunderstorm cloud.
The continuous movement of water through the environment: evaporation (liquid to gas) → condensation (gas to liquid/clouds) → precipitation (rain/snow) → collection (rivers/oceans) → repeat.
The boundary between two air masses of different temperatures. Cold fronts (cold air pushing warm air) bring sudden storms. Warm fronts (warm air pushing cold air) bring gradual rain.
Lines on a weather map connecting points of equal air pressure. Closely spaced isobars mean strong winds; widely spaced isobars mean light winds.
A scale from 0-12 for estimating wind speed based on visible effects: 0 = calm (smoke rises vertically), 6 = strong breeze (large branches move), 12 = hurricane.
An instrument that measures atmospheric pressure. Rising pressure usually indicates fair weather approaching; falling pressure often indicates storms or rain coming.
Any form of water falling from clouds to the ground — rain, snow, sleet, or hail. Precipitation type depends on temperature at different altitudes.
Weather is the short-term atmospheric conditions (today's temperature and rain). Climate is the long-term average weather pattern for a region over 30+ years.

endings.title: Weather Master
endings.message: You have achieved mastery at the Weather Station! Your meteorology knowledge is extraordinary, your forecasts are trusted by the entire school community, and your data collection rivals professional weather services. Mr. Cirrus nominates you for the Young Meteorologist Award, and the visiting professional invites you to tour the national weather service center. You have proven that understanding the atmosphere empowers you to protect and serve your community!

endings.title: Skilled Forecaster
endings.message: You have become a skilled weather forecaster with solid meteorology knowledge! Your Showcase presentation demonstrated real understanding of atmospheric science. Mr. Cirrus says you are ready for the advanced earth science elective next year. Your forecasts have already helped the school community, and your future in science is bright!

endings.title: Weather Watcher
endings.message: You completed the Weather Station program with growing confidence. Some concepts were challenging and not every forecast was correct, but you stuck with it and learned the fundamentals of meteorology. Mr. Cirrus says there is always next semester to sharpen your skills. Keep watching the sky — every great meteorologist started by simply looking up!

endings.title: Struggling Observer
endings.message: The Weather Station was a tough journey for you. Weather science has a lot of moving parts, and connecting them all into accurate forecasts is genuinely hard. But you never stopped trying. Mr. Cirrus arranges extra sessions and says: 'The atmosphere is the most complex system on Earth. Struggling with it means you are engaging with real science.' Your story is just beginning!

endings.title: Station in Trouble
endings.message: The weather station has suffered from poor maintenance and unreliable forecasts this semester. Community trust has dropped and the instruments need serious repair. It is a hard lesson, but Mr. Cirrus reminds you: 'Even the best meteorologists have bad seasons. What matters is rebuilding — recalibrating your instruments, restoring trust, and trying again.' Breezy is already planning the maintenance schedule for next semester.

An organism that makes its own food

questions.explanation: Producers (like plants) make their own food through photosynthesis.

questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and minerals from soil and anchor the plant.
